RagShortTexts: The Sachsenspiegel codified Saxon customary and feudal law into German vernacular text.

Variants.Content: Eike von Repgow compiled the Sachsenspiegel, the most authoritative vernacular record of German customary law. Its two parts, the Landrecht for civil matters and the Lehnrecht for feudal obligations, set out how the imperial electors were chosen, what knights owed in military service, and how free tenure was held. Written in German rather than Latin, the book reached lords and judges who never read the older legal texts. Its rules did not come from a single ruler's decree, but from the practice of local courts that had long kept the peace.

Under the Lehnrecht, a liege lord could not strip a vassal of his fief without a judicial ruling. Knight service could not be pushed past six weeks unless the lord paid for the extra time. Such rules shielded the lesser nobility from ducal encroachment, and a count who ignored them risked losing his vassals to the courts.
The Landrecht guards our boundary stones; not even a baron may remove a village mark without trial. Burdened as we are, customary law prevents the manor steward from inventing arbitrary new levies.
